summary.title: Northstar cloud AI assistant
summary.description:
Assumptions:
- Ticket service is part of the portal
- staff approval takes place inside the portal UI
- audit events do not include who approved or denied a certain action
- the data processing agreement of LLM providers is undefined
- the sign-in of staff members does not require MFA
- the portal lacks file upload quotas on both size and number

threats.title: B04: An attacker phishes a staff member's credentials and signs in as them
threats.description: In the scenario when an attacker is able to seize the credentials of a staff member through whatever means, the attacker is subsequently able to access all tenant information available to that specific staff member. Since the identity provider (P1) forwards a validated token to the portal (P2), the attacker is recognized by the portal as a staff member and has all of their permissions and access.
threats.mitigation: To mitigate this, controls can be put into place for credential management. The most obvious mitigation is to introduce MFA for all staff members on the identity provider (P1). Additionally, anomaly sign-in detection and device attestation would provide more checks to validate the staff members identity. With these checks in place, it is less likely that an attacker could breach a staff members account and assume their permissions.

threats.title: B03: Approvals aren't linked to a specific staff member
threats.description: Staff members have the final sign-off on whether or not a tool gateway execution is accepted or denied. Despite this, and despite the presence of an audit log, there is no observability into which staff member approved or denied each action. Therefore, in the wake of an incident caused by poor judgement or malicious intent, the staff member responsible cannot be directly traced back to.
threats.mitigation: To mitigate this, it should be required that the tool gateway (P4) sends a record of all permission decisions and the staff member with the final decision to S3. With this in place, all decisions can be directly attributed to a staff member. For further security, it's essential that records within the store cannot be modified or deleted in order to maintain a source of truth.

threats.title: B02: Sensitive data is sent to the external LLM provider and potentially stored there
threats.description: Since Northstar relies on an external LLM provider (P3) to return generated responses, the organization's surface area for attacks becomes larger if the LLM provider stores or retains tenant prompts and information. In the case that the external LLM provider does retain information for various reasons, then a breach of the provider is also capable of exposing internal tenant data.
threats.mitigation: This threat can be best mitigated contractually. When choosing an LLM provider, Northstar should aim to choose solutions that provide either a "no-retention" policy, or provide room to negotiate retention conditions. With this in place, internal tenant data isn't stored by the LLM provider, so a breach to the provider does not expose any Northstar-specific information.

threats.title: B01: Malicious documents carry prompt-injection text
threats.description: A critical threat to Northstar's operations is the threat of prompt injection by the upload of malicious documents. An attacker would be able to meticulously design PDFs with hidden instructions aimed to exploit an LLM's behaviour that would be entrusted as a genuine document by the system. This means that the malicious document would follow the entire system flow of indexing and retrieval. Consequently, results could be "poisoned" by the malicious documents, causing assistant summaries to be incorrect or dangerous actions to be taken.

threats.title: B05: Many large documents get the Ingestion Worker stuck processing them
threats.description: A malicious actor could upload a large quantity of huge documents in an attempt to bog down or stop the ingestion worker. Under the assumption that the ingestion worker processes documents sequentially in a queue without preempting anything, then the malicious documents would continue to occupy the ingestion worker without letting genuine documents begin processing. The consequence of this is that genuine documents are delayed or never indexed and therefore downstream responses could be inaccurate or incomplete.
threats.mitigation: This threat can be addressed in two pivotal places. First, P5 could have a safeguard that rejects documents, or rather, batches of documents that exceed some well-defined size criterion. Second, P7 could be improved (under our assumptions of its nature) to preempt the processing of files that exceed some predefined time. This way, massive documents are outright rejected, and no single document occupies too much of P7's attention.
